refuted.title: Path containment check removed from hooks remove/edit allows escape from hooks dir
refuted.description:
This change deletes the only containment check that kept a hook filename inside the hooks directory. The baseline computed `filepath.Abs(hookFile)` and rejected the operation with "hook file %s is outside of hookDir %s" unless the resolved path stayed under `hooksDir`; both copies of that check (in `removeHooksCmd` and in `editHooksCmd`) are removed here.

`hookFileName` comes straight from `args[0]` and is concatenated into the path with no cleaning, no `filepath.Clean`, and no separator rejection:

    hookFileName := args[0]
    hookFile = preInstallHooksDir + "/" + hookFileName

A value containing `../` therefore resolves outside `/etc/uniget/hooks/...` (or `$HOME/.config/uniget/hooks/...` in `--user` mode) and is passed directly to `os.Remove` at line 171. The same root cause affects `editHooksCmd`, where the unconstrained `hookFile` is handed to the spawned editor (line 226-227) and then to `os.Chmod(hookFile, 0700)` at line 236 — so an escaping path yields arbitrary file content modification plus a mode change to root-only 0700 on any file the process can reach. I searched `cmd/uniget` for any remaining `filepath.Abs`/`Clean`/`Rel` or prefix check and found none, so nothing downstream re-establishes the boundary.

Note that the other checks this commit removes (the `os.Lstat(hookFile); if err == nil` "is a symlink" guards in `editHooksCmd` and `processHooks`) were genuinely broken — `Lstat` succeeds for any existing file, so they rejected every real hook — and removing those is a correctness fix, not a regression. The `hooksDir` prefix check is different: it was correct and load-bearing, and it is gone.

I could not establish a privilege boundary from the code in this snapshot: only `cmd/uniget` is tracked here, there is no setuid/`sudo` re-exec anywhere in the tree, and the traversal input is the invoking operator's own argv. The exposure is therefore real but conditional — it matters where `uniget` runs with privileges the argv supplier does not have (a constrained sudoers entry scoped to `uniget hooks *`, a CI job or automation that templates a hook name from a variable, or a root-run wrapper). Confidence is medium for that reason: the source-to-sink chain is fully read, the escalation context is not visible from here.
refuted.exploit_scenario: Where `uniget` is invoked with privileges above those of whoever supplies the hook name — e.g. a sudoers rule restricting a user to `uniget hooks *`, or CI automation that builds the hook name from a job variable — the supplier passes `uniget hooks remove --type pre-install ../../../../etc/cron.d/somejob`. `hookFile` becomes `/etc/uniget/hooks/pre-install.d/../../../../etc/cron.d/somejob`, `fileExists` confirms it, and `os.Remove` at line 171 deletes it as root. Using `hooks edit` with the same argument instead opens `/etc/cron.d/somejob` in the operator's `$EDITOR` for arbitrary rewriting and then applies `os.Chmod(..., 0700)` to it. Before this change both attempts were rejected with "hook file ... is outside of hookDir ...".

verification.reason: 1 of 3 verifier(s) never reported, so the panel could not settle this and the finding stands as reported — The factual half of the claim is accurate — the diff does delete the `filepath.Abs` + `strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, hooksDir)` containment check from both `removeHooksCmd` and `editHooksCmd` (cmd/uniget/hooks.go, removed hunks at the old lines preceding the current 165-171 and 226-236), and `hookFileName` from `args[0]` now reaches `os.Remove`/`exec.Command`/`os.Chmod` uncleaned. What fails is the impact: the sole source is the invoking operator's own argv of a local CLI, so with no privilege boundary the "attack" is deleting a file the caller could already delete with `rm`. The only boundary the reviewer posits (a sudoers rule scoped to `uniget hooks *`, or CI templating a hook name) is self-defeating: the untouched, pre-existing `testHookCmd` at cmd/uniget/hooks.go:338-355 concatenates `args[0]` into `hookFile` with no containment at all and hands it to `runHook` → `exec.Command(hookFile, ...)` at line 383, and `hooks add --source /any/file` + `hooks run` does the same — both give arbitrary root code execution in exactly that scenario, without this change. The removed check was also only a string-prefix test that a sibling path such as `/etc/uniget-old/x` already satisfied, so it was never a sound boundary. Searched: I looked for anything that would re-establish the boundary or, failing that, a privilege boundary that would make the traversal meaningful. (1) Searched cmd/uniget for `filepath.Abs|Clean|Rel` and prefix checks — confirmed via get_diff that both copies are deleted and `path/filepath` is dropped from the imports, so the reviewer is right that no containment remains. (2) Searched the whole tree for `setuid|Setuid|sudo|Geteuid|http.ListenAndServe|http.Handle` — no matches, no daemon, no privileged re-exec; the repo tracks only cmd/uniget (list_directory on root, depth 2), and `search_code 'hooks (remove|edit|rm|del)'` finds no CI/script caller that templates a hook name. (3) Checked whether the argv supplier is already trusted with more: `--prefix`/`--user` are rootCmd persistent flags (cmd/uniget/main.go:412-414) settable by the same caller, and the unchanged `testHookCmd` (hooks.go:338-355) and `add`+`run` paths already exec attacker-named files as the process user with no containment. (4) Verified via git_log that hooks.go has only two commits (baseline + this change), so the removed check was not a response to a known incident.

votes.reasoning: The factual half of the claim is accurate — the diff does delete the `filepath.Abs` + `strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, hooksDir)` containment check from both `removeHooksCmd` and `editHooksCmd` (cmd/uniget/hooks.go, removed hunks at the old lines preceding the current 165-171 and 226-236), and `hookFileName` from `args[0]` now reaches `os.Remove`/`exec.Command`/`os.Chmod` uncleaned. What fails is the impact: the sole source is the invoking operator's own argv of a local CLI, so with no privilege boundary the "attack" is deleting a file the caller could already delete with `rm`. The only boundary the reviewer posits (a sudoers rule scoped to `uniget hooks *`, or CI templating a hook name) is self-defeating: the untouched, pre-existing `testHookCmd` at cmd/uniget/hooks.go:338-355 concatenates `args[0]` into `hookFile` with no containment at all and hands it to `runHook` → `exec.Command(hookFile, ...)` at line 383, and `hooks add --source /any/file` + `hooks run` does the same — both give arbitrary root code execution in exactly that scenario, without this change. The removed check was also only a string-prefix test that a sibling path such as `/etc/uniget-old/x` already satisfied, so it was never a sound boundary.

The removal of the `filepath.Abs` + `strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, hooksDir)` guard in `removeHooksCmd`/`editHooksCmd` is real (diff, cmd/uniget/hooks.go), but the "source" is the operator's own argv of a local, non-setuid CLI: I searched cmd/uniget for `Setuid`/`Geteuid`/`http.`/`ListenAndServe` and found no daemon, no network entry point, and no privilege re-exec anywhere in the tracked tree, so `os.Remove` at line 171 runs with exactly the privileges of whoever typed the command — deleting a file they could already delete with `rm`. The only escalation premise the reviewer offers (a sudoers rule scoped to `uniget hooks *` or CI templating) is already fully broken by code this MR does not touch: `testHookCmd` (hooks.go:296-317) builds `hookFile` from `args[0]` with no containment at all and hands it to `runHook` → `exec.Command(hookFile, ...)`, and `addHooksCmd` + `runHooksCmd` let any caller drop an executable into the hooks dir (chmod 0700) and run it — both give arbitrary code execution as the invoking (root) user before and after this change, so the deleted check adds no marginal protection in the one scenario where a boundary would exist. The change is a defense-in-depth/robustness regression worth flagging in review, not an exploitable path traversal.

refuted.title: Path containment check removed from `hooks remove`/`hooks edit`
refuted.description:
This change deletes the only control that confined hook operations to the hooks directory. Both `removeHooksCmd` and `editHooksCmd` previously did:

    hookFileAbs, err := filepath.Abs(hookFile)
    if !strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, hooksDir) { return ...outside of hookDir... }

`hookFile` is built by naive string concatenation from `hookFileName := args[0]` (line 146 for remove, line 203 for edit) onto `hooksDir` (`viper.GetString("prefix") + "/" + configDirectory`, which is absolute — `/etc/uniget` in system mode — so the deleted check was functional, not dead code). With the check gone, a value such as `../../../../etc/cron.d/job` escapes the hooks tree and reaches `os.Remove(hookFile)` at line 171, and in `editHooksCmd` reaches `exec.Command(editorWithArgs[0], ...)` followed by `os.Chmod(hookFile, 0700)` at line 236 — arbitrary file deletion, an arbitrary file opened in the invoker's editor, and an arbitrary path chmod'ed to 0700.

Two related hardening removals in the same commit, which I am not reporting separately: the `os.Lstat` symlink rejection in `processHooks` (now line 425-426), which was meant to stop a symlink planted in `/etc/uniget/hooks/*.d` from being executed by `runHook`; and the change at line 199 from `strings.Split(editor, " ")[0]` to passing the full split of `$UNIGET_EDITOR`/`$EDITOR` as argv. Both removed `Lstat` checks were in fact broken — `err == nil` is true for any existing file, not only symlinks — so deleting them restores functionality that previously always failed.

Confidence is low deliberately: I could not close the trust boundary. `args[0]`, `$EDITOR` and `$UNIGET_PREFIX` are all supplied by the same principal that runs the binary, the hook directories are created root-owned 0755 by `assertDirectory`, and no code path I could find feeds these arguments from a less-privileged source. Under `sudo` the environment is scrubbed by default. So this is a removed hardening control rather than a demonstrated privilege crossing, and it is flagged for a human to weigh rather than asserted as exploitable.
refuted.exploit_scenario: A caller who can invoke the binary but is expected to be constrained to managing hooks — for example an automation wrapper or a sudoers rule scoped to `uniget hooks *` — runs `uniget hooks remove --type pre-install ../../../../etc/cron.d/uniget`. The path is concatenated unchecked onto `/etc/uniget/hooks/pre-install.d/`, resolves outside the hooks tree, and `os.Remove` deletes the file with the process's privileges. The same argument to `hooks edit` opens an arbitrary path in the editor and then chmods it to 0700. Note that the `pre-install` branch of `removeHooksCmd` (lines 150-152) does not even call `assertDirectory`, so nothing else touches the path first.

verification.reason: 3/3 verifier(s) agreed — The diff does delete the `filepath.Abs`/`strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, hooksDir)` containment check from both `removeHooksCmd` and `editHooksCmd` (cmd/uniget/hooks.go, removed block before line 168 and before line 236), so the reviewer's reading of the code is accurate. What fails is the trust boundary: the only source is `args[0]` of a local cobra CLI command (`hooks.go:146`, `hooks.go:203`), registered only on `rootCmd` via `initHooksCmd` (`hooks.go:41,48`), and the process runs with exactly the privileges of whoever typed the command — `search_code` for `setuid|sudoers|NOPASSWD|4755` returned nothing, `cmd/uniget/` contains no server/daemon/API surface, and there is no in-repo caller that feeds `hooks remove`/`hooks edit` from a less-privileged source. Removing a file, or opening and chmod'ing one, that the invoking principal could already `rm`/`chmod` directly is not a privilege crossing; the claimed impact rests entirely on a hypothetical `uniget hooks *`-scoped sudoers rule that exists nowhere in the repository, and `--prefix`/`$HOME`/`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` are controlled by the same principal anyway, so the deleted check never bounded a security boundary — it was self-consistency hardening. Searched: I looked for anything that would make `args[0]` cross a privilege boundary or be supplied by a party other than the invoker. (1) `search_code` for `removeHooksCmd|editHooksCmd` — only 8 hits, all in cmd/uniget/hooks.go (flag registration lines 36-48 and the command definitions at 132/180); no programmatic caller anywhere. (2) `search_code` for `hooks (remove|edit|rm|add)` across the repo — no matches, so no script, CI job, or wrapper shells out to these subcommands with externally-sourced arguments. (3) `search_code` for `setuid|sudoers|NOPASSWD|chmod \+?s|4755` — no matches, so the binary is not installed privileged and no restricted sudo policy ships with it. (4) `list_directory cmd/uniget` — 26 files, all local package-manager subcommands (install, uninstall, cache, search, ...); there is no server, daemon, or RPC entry point that could deliver an attacker-supplied hook name. (5) I confirmed via cmd/uniget/main.go:93-147 that `prefix`/`configDirectory` are derived from the invoker's own `--prefix` flag and `$HOME`/`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, i.e. the same principal controls both sides of the comparison the removed check performed. I also verified the removed check was functional (hooksDir is absolute in both system and `--user` mode), so the finding is factually right about the code and wrong only about there being a security boundary to cross.

votes.reasoning: The diff does delete the `filepath.Abs`/`strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, hooksDir)` containment check from both `removeHooksCmd` and `editHooksCmd` (cmd/uniget/hooks.go, removed block before line 168 and before line 236), so the reviewer's reading of the code is accurate. What fails is the trust boundary: the only source is `args[0]` of a local cobra CLI command (`hooks.go:146`, `hooks.go:203`), registered only on `rootCmd` via `initHooksCmd` (`hooks.go:41,48`), and the process runs with exactly the privileges of whoever typed the command — `search_code` for `setuid|sudoers|NOPASSWD|4755` returned nothing, `cmd/uniget/` contains no server/daemon/API surface, and there is no in-repo caller that feeds `hooks remove`/`hooks edit` from a less-privileged source. Removing a file, or opening and chmod'ing one, that the invoking principal could already `rm`/`chmod` directly is not a privilege crossing; the claimed impact rests entirely on a hypothetical `uniget hooks *`-scoped sudoers rule that exists nowhere in the repository, and `--prefix`/`$HOME`/`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` are controlled by the same principal anyway, so the deleted check never bounded a security boundary — it was self-consistency hardening.

The removal is real (diff on cmd/uniget/hooks.go deletes the `filepath.Abs` + `strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, hooksDir)` guard from both `removeHooksCmd` and `editHooksCmd`), but the only source for `hookFileName` is `args[0]` of a locally-invoked cobra CLI (`cmd/uniget/hooks.go:146`, `:203`); I searched the whole repo for any non-argv caller (`search_code` for `removeHooksCmd|editHooksCmd`, and for any HTTP/RPC server — no `http.ListenAndServe`, no daemon, no setuid/4755 anywhere), so the value is supplied by the same principal that already owns the process's privileges. The reviewer's only privilege-crossing scenario (a wrapper or sudoers rule scoped to `uniget hooks *`) is already fully defeated by unchanged code in the same subcommand group: `testHookCmd` at cmd/uniget/hooks.go:346-355 concatenates `args[0]` onto the hooks dir with no containment check ever and passes it to `runHook` → `exec.Command`, giving arbitrary binary execution, and `addHooksCmd` (lines 94-127) + `hooks run` lets any source file be copied in, chmod'ed 0700 and executed. The deleted guard therefore protected no boundary that the untouched code does not already leave wide open — it is defense-in-depth churn in a single-principal CLI, not a demonstrated path-traversal vulnerability.

Working backwards from the sink: `os.Remove(hookFile)` at cmd/uniget/hooks.go:171 (and the `exec.Command`/`os.Chmod` at 231-236) is reached only from the cobra `RunE` of `uniget hooks remove`/`hooks edit`; a repo-wide search for other callers (`removeHooksCmd|editHooksCmd|hooks (remove|edit)`) finds only the registrations at hooks.go:36-48, so the sole source of `args[0]` is the argv of the person invoking the binary, acting with that process's own privileges — deleting/chmod'ing a file you already have rights to is not a privilege crossing. The claim's only non-trivial threat model, a principal confined to `uniget hooks *`, is refuted by unmodified code in the same file: `testHookCmd` (hooks.go:340-355) concatenates `args[0]` onto the hooks dir with no containment check at all and passes it to `runHook` → `exec.Command(hookFile, ...)` (hooks.go:443), and `addHooksCmd` (hooks.go:88-127) plus `hooks run` let that same principal drop and execute a script as the invoking user; neither was touched by this diff, so such a principal already has arbitrary execution and the removed `HasPrefix` check bought nothing. The removal at hooks.go:159-166 of the baseline is real and is a defense-in-depth regression worth a maintainer's note, but the chain's impact link (a security consequence beyond what the same caller can already do) does not close.
